advisories.title: Login V2 exposes internal functions as unauthenticated endpoints
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s **Login V2** UI made several internal server-side functions callable from the outside without authentication. These functions were only meant to be used by the Login UI itself, and they ran with the Login V2 service account, which has instance-wide permissions.

The functions accepted the user they act on, the link they send by email, or the session lifetime directly from the request. Login V2 did not check that the caller was signed in as that user or allowed to choose those values.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who knows a user’s ID can:

* **Take over accounts that have not set up an authentication method yet**, such as invited users who have not accepted their invite. ZITADEL sends the user a genuine verification or invite email, but with a link to a host the attacker controls. When the link is opened - by the user or by an automated link scanner - the attacker receives the code and can set the account’s first credential.
* **Mark the user as having skipped the MFA setup prompt.** In **Login V1**, this hides the optional prompt to set up a second factor for the skip period configured in the login policy. It does **not** bypass MFA that is enforced by the login policy or already set up, and **Login V2** does not act on the flag.
* **View the user’s session details** (login name, display name and verified factors) on the account selection page, if they also know the ID of one of the user’s sessions.

A user who is signed in through **Login V2** can also **choose the lifetime of their own session**, overriding the check lifetimes configured in the login policy.

This affects deployments that serve the hosted **Login V2** UI. Deployments that do not run Login V2 are not affected.

The ZITADEL APIs themselves enforced their permissions correctly; the requests were authorized as the Login V2 service account. Accounts that already have an authentication method are **not** taken over this way: the email code then only verifies the email address. A session viewed on the account selection page can **not** be used or changed, because every action on it still requires its session token. Revoking a session and deactivating a user still take effect regardless of the chosen lifetime.

**Scope note:** This affects only the **Login V2** UI. Each attack stays within the instance the Login V2 deployment serves, but reaches users of every organization in that instance. Viewing another user’s session details is a further way around the protection added in GHSA-jh92-5mrj-p2w2.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

**Login V2** now only makes the functions its pages need callable, and checks this when it is built. Each of them takes the user and session from the caller’s own signed session cookie, email links are built by the server, and session lifetimes always come from the login policy.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to Lucas Dodgson from InfoGuard Labs ([@lucasdodgson](https://github.com/lucasdodgson)) for finding and reporting the vulnerability.

advisories.title: Login V2: authentication bypass via unauthenticated (zero-factor) session for OIDC and SAML requests
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL issued tokens or a SAML response for an OIDC or SAML authorization request without ensuring that the session used to complete the request had been authenticated to the request’s requirements by an authorized login client. Completing a request is meant to be performed only by a login client holding the `session.link` permission, which is responsible for verifying the session first. That guarantee was not enforced, and the gap was reachable through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** and directly through the completion endpoints.

Through the hosted **Login V2**, a request could be completed with a session on which no authentication factor had been verified: an unauthenticated attacker who knows a victim’s login name could obtain tokens or a SAML response for that user when the user has two or more linked identity providers, or when the organization disables local authentication and offers two or more identity providers - both possible under the default login policy.

The same missing guarantee was reachable directly through the **OIDC Service** (`CreateCallback`) and **SAML Service** (`CreateResponse`) completion endpoints, which trusted the `x-zitadel-login-client` header to identify the login client. ZITADEL records this header from the *unauthenticated* authorization request without validating it, so any authenticated user of the instance could name themselves as the login client and complete a request for a session whose ID and token they hold - again without holding the `session.link` permission that completion requires.

In both cases the root cause is the same: request completion did not require an authorized login client - one holding `session.link` - to have verified that the session satisfied the request’s authentication requirements. Only deployments that authenticate users through ZITADEL (OIDC/SAML) are affected.

### Impact

An attacker who can complete a request as described can:

- **Obtain tokens or a SAML response for a victim** and sign in as that user at any OIDC or SAML application of the instance that trusts it, including when the login policy (for example enforced **MFA**) was not satisfied or no factor was verified at all. The attacker chooses the `client_id`, so any such application in the instance can be targeted, and the registered redirect URI does not limit the attack because the authorization code is returned to the attacker directly.
- **Take over accounts** at relying parties that use public clients (SPA, native or mobile apps using PKCE) and at clients registered for the implicit or hybrid flow, and at SAML service providers.
- **Read the victim’s profile claims** from the userinfo endpoint.

Reaching the gap through the hosted **Login V2** requires only knowledge of the victim’s login name. Reaching it directly through the completion endpoints additionally requires an account on the instance and a session the attacker already holds for the victim - the issue does **not** allow creating sessions for other users, which still requires the `session.write` permission.

Device authorization and failing a SAML request were **not** affected, as both always required `session.link`. Confidential clients that use only the authorization code flow are protected by client authentication when the code is redeemed, and ZITADEL’s own management APIs and Console reject tokens issued for a session with no verified factor.

**Scope note:** Impact is limited to a single instance (no cross‑instance impact). The two attack surfaces are the same missing check on request completion, closed together in the patched release.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

advisories.title: Session API and Login V2: organization login policy not enforced for password sign-in
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL allowed anyone who knows the password of a user to sign in with it through **Login V2** and the **Session API**, even when the user’s organization has disabled local authentication (username and password) and requires sign-in through an external identity provider.

Login V2 checked this setting at the login name step. Its password step, however, did not reliably check it against the user’s own organization. The Session API (`CreateSession` and `SetSession`, v2 and v2beta) accepted password checks without reading the login policy. In both vectors, a password sign-in was never checked against the login policy of the user’s own organization.

### Impact

An attacker who knows the password of a user in an organization with local authentication disabled can:

* **Sign in with username and password** through Login V2 and get a valid session for every application that uses ZITADEL for sign-in.
* **Bypass the controls of the external identity provider** that the organization relies on, such as its multi-factor authentication, conditional access or device checks.
* **Keep signing in after being offboarded at the identity provider**, as long as the user is still active in ZITADEL and has a password.
* **Sign in through custom login UIs** built on the **Session API** that do not check this setting themselves.

This affects organizations that disable local authentication while some of their users still have a password in ZITADEL, for example a password set before the organization moved to an external identity provider.

The issue does **not** bypass the password itself: the password is still verified, and failed attempts still count toward the lockout policy. The impact is that a known or leaked password defeats the identity provider controls the organization requires. Users without a password are not affected, as no local credential is involved. **Login V1** is not affected, as it checks the login policy of the user’s own organization.

**Scope note:** The vulnerability is limited to password sign-in through Login V2 and the Session API, for users of the affected instance. It is an incomplete fix of [GHSA-25rw-g6ff-fmg8](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-25rw-g6ff-fmg8) (CVE-2026-29193), which enforced this setting on the Login V2 server but did not cover every password sign-in path.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

ZITADEL now checks the login policy of the user’s own organization for every password check through the Session API, and Login V2 checks the same setting at its password step. If the user’s organization or its login policy cannot be determined, the password check is refused.

Password checks for users in organizations with local authentication disabled now fail with `FAILED_PRECONDITION` (`Errors.Org.LoginPolicy.UsernamePasswordNotAllowed`). This also applies when such a user signs in through an application of another organization that allows local authentication, the same as in Login V1. These users can also no longer change their password with their current password in Login V2. Custom login UIs built on the Session API should send these users to their external identity provider.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to Robert Capps from Stratovera LLC ([@rwcii](https://github.com/rwcii)) for finding and reporting the vulnerability.

advisories.title: Login V2: external IdP sign-in callback not bound to the initiating browser (login CSRF / session swapping)
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI did not bind an external identity‑provider (IdP) sign‑in to the browser that started it. An attacker could get a victim’s browser to finish an external IdP sign‑in that the attacker had started with their own account, so that the victim ended up signed in to the **attacker’s** ZITADEL account. This is commonly called login CSRF, session swapping, or account pre‑hijacking.

The sign‑in was completed without verifying that the browser finishing it was the same browser that started it.

### Impact

An attacker who can sign in to the instance with their own external IdP identity can:

* **Place a victim into the attacker’s account** when the victim opens a link from the attacker, with no further interaction.
* **Collect what the victim then does under that identity**: data the victim enters, documents they upload, and integrations or authentication methods they configure all land in the attacker‑controlled account and can be retrieved by the attacker later.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML) with at least one external identity provider configured.

On its own the issue does **not** expose the victim’s existing account, data, or credentials, because the victim is signed in to the attacker’s account rather than the reverse. It requires the victim to open an attacker‑supplied link inside a time window (the external provider’s authorization‑code window, or otherwise the intent lifetime, `1h` by default). Deployments that enforce multi‑factor authentication interrupt the automatic sign‑in at the factor step. ZITADEL’s **Login V1** UI is **not** affected, because it binds the external login to the browser that started it. Instances that do **not** use external identity providers are **not** affected, because no IdP intent is ever issued.

**Scope note:** The affected surface is external‑IdP sign‑in through **Login V2**. The exposure is instance‑wide and spans organizations wherever Login V2 and an external IdP are in use; it is not cross‑instance. This concerns the same external‑login intent flow as [GHSA-jh3m-cr2x-qp88](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-jh3m-cr2x-qp88), but a different missing check: that advisory addressed forgeable intent tokens, while this one concerns binding the completed callback to the browser that began the flow.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

The patched **Login V2** now verifies that the browser completing an external IdP sign‑in is the same browser that started the flow, and rejects a callback presented by any other browser. A legitimate same‑browser sign‑in is unaffected.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions. Enforcing multi‑factor authentication is a partial mitigation only: it interrupts the automatic sign‑in at the factor step, but does not restore the missing browser binding.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

This vulnerability was found by [zentrust partners GmbH](https://zentrust.partners/) during a scheduled penetration test. Thank you to the analysts Martin Tschirsich and Joud Zakharia.

The full report will be made public after the complete review.

advisories.title: Login V2: Arbitrary Redirect URL Accepted
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI allowed an unauthenticated attacker to craft a link on the instance’s own domain whose “Back to Login” button leads to an attacker-controlled website. Two error pages that Login V2 shows after a sign-in with an external identity provider took the destination of that button from the link itself, without checking that it points back into the login UI.

### Impact

An attacker who can send a link to a victim can:

* **Craft a phishing link on the trusted ZITADEL domain** that shows a genuine, branded “account not found” or “registration failed” page and whose “Back to Login” button navigates to a site of the attacker’s choice.
* **Show an organization’s branding on the page**, so it looks like the victim’s usual login.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML).

The issue does **not** leak any session, token, code or other secret: the navigation to the attacker’s site is a plain click on a link and carries nothing from the ZITADEL origin. It does not redirect automatically; the victim must open the crafted link and then click the button. It does not allow script execution on the ZITADEL origin. Deployments that serve only **Login V1** are not affected, as the vulnerable pages exist only in Login V2. No identity provider needs to be configured for the pages to render.

**Scope note:** This affects the **Login V2** UI only. The crafted link works on any instance that serves Login V2, across organizations, but not across instances. It is unrelated to [GHSA-6rx5-m2rc-hmf7](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-6rx5-m2rc-hmf7) and [GHSA-5wcj-9wj4-j65h](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-5wcj-9wj4-j65h), which concern the administrator-configured default redirect URI, a different setting.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.5.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

The patched version only shows the “Back to Login” button when its destination is a page of the login UI itself. For any other destination, including other websites, the page is shown without the button.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

This vulnerability was found by [zentrust partners GmbH](https://zentrust.partners/) during a scheduled penetration test. Thank you to the analysts Martin Tschirsich and Joud Zakharia.

The full report will be made public after the complete review.

advisories.title: Login V2: opening a link adds an OTP email or SMS second factor to a signed-in user without confirmation
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI let an attacker add a second factor to the account of a signed‑in user by getting them to open a link. A user with an authenticated Login V2 session who opened the setup page for one of these factors - for example through a link or redirect from another site - had **OTP‑Email** or **OTP‑SMS** added to their account, without any confirmation.

The page added the factor while it was being loaded, instead of in response to an explicit action of the user, so it could not tell a deliberate enrolment from one triggered by another site.

### Impact

An attacker who can get a signed‑in user to open a link can:

* **Add OTP‑Email** as a second factor to the user’s account, if the user has a verified email address.
* **Add OTP‑SMS** as a second factor to the user’s account, if the user has a verified phone number.

This affects deployments that serve ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI.

The issue does **not** give the attacker access to the account, to any credential, or to the one‑time codes: the added factor sends its codes to the user’s own verified email address or phone number. The user also sees the page confirming the new factor. The real impact is on the integrity of the user’s authentication setup: an account that previously offered only stronger factors, such as passkeys, additionally accepts a code sent by email or SMS, which an attacker who later obtains the password can try to phish. The page only acted on sessions that are already authenticated; a session that merely identifies a user by login name is rejected. Users without a verified email address or phone number cannot have the corresponding factor added, and a factor that is already set up is not changed. Setting up **TOTP** through the same page is **not** affected, because it only takes effect after the user enters a code from their authenticator app. ZITADEL’s **Login V1** UI is **not** affected, because it only adds these factors as a step of the user’s own ongoing sign‑in.

**Scope note:** The affected surface is second‑factor setup in **Login V2**. The exposure is limited to users who are signed in to Login V2 in the browser that opens the link; it is not cross‑instance. The ZITADEL APIs themselves are not affected.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

The patched **Login V2** no longer adds a second factor when the setup page is opened. It asks the user to confirm, and only adds **OTP‑Email** or **OTP‑SMS** after the user explicitly does so. If the factor cannot be added, the page now shows an error instead of reporting success.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions. Removing **OTP‑Email** and **OTP‑SMS** from the second factors allowed in the login settings only limits which factors users are offered; it does not prevent the page from adding them.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to the security researcher who found and reported the vulnerability; they asked not to be named.

advisories.title: Login V1: Authentication bypass in the OIDC authorization code flow
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V1** UI allowed an attacker who can sign in to an instance with their own account, and who knows a victim’s login name, to obtain OIDC tokens for the victim without the victim’s credentials.

Authorization codes issued at the end of a **Login V1** sign-in were not reliably bound to the user who completed that sign-in, so the token endpoint could issue tokens for a user who had not authenticated.

### Impact

An attacker who can complete a **Login V1** sign-in with their own account and knows a victim’s login name can:

* **Sign in to an OIDC application as the victim** - the application receives an ID token, an access token, a refresh token if requested, and userinfo for the victim.
* **Bypass all of the victim’s authentication** - none of the victim’s factors (**password, passkeys, TOTP, OTP-SMS, OTP-Email, U2F**) or external identity provider sign-ins are checked.
* **Act with the victim’s roles and grants** in that application.
* **Use the victim’s ZITADEL permissions** when the application requests access to the ZITADEL APIs - for example the ZITADEL Console when it signs in through **Login V1**. If the victim is an administrator, this includes administrative access to the organization or instance.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V1** UI using the OIDC authorization code flow.

The attacker needs a working account of their own that can sign in through the same login. No interaction from the victim is required, and the victim is not notified. The attack does **not** reveal the victim’s password or other credentials; its impact is the issued tokens and everything they grant. SAML applications, the OIDC implicit flow, and applications that sign in through **Login V2** are **not** affected by this issue.

**Scope note:** This affects the **Login V1** UI and the OIDC authorization code flow only. Within an instance, it reaches any user the login can find by login name, including users of other organizations unless the login is restricted to one organization. It does not reach across instances.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

An authorization code issued through **Login V1** is now bound to the user who completed the sign-in, and tokens are only issued for that user while their sign-in is still valid. Codes that were issued but not yet redeemed before the upgrade are rejected; the affected users sign in again.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.20.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.20.3)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to Lucas Dodgson from InfoGuard Labs ([@lucasdodgson](https://github.com/lucasdodgson)) for finding and reporting the vulnerability.

advisories.title: Bypass of GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76: account takeover via userinfo in the public host header
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL allowed an unauthenticated attacker who knows only a victim’s login name to redirect that victim’s genuine password-reset, invite, and email-verification links to an attacker-controlled host, while the links still carried the real single-use codes. Harvesting such a code lets the attacker set a new password - or complete verification - and sign in as the victim, including an instance administrator. This is a bypass of the fix for [GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76).

The fix for GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76 validates the public host from the `x-zitadel-public-host` request header against the instance’s trusted domains. However, the trusted-domain check and the links read the header value differently: a value that places a trusted host in the user-information portion of the header, in front of an attacker-controlled host, was checked as the trusted host, while a link built from the same value points to the attacker host. The shared missing invariant is that the host checked against the trusted domains is not guaranteed to be the host the resulting links point to.

### Impact

An attacker who can reach the unauthenticated password-reset or verification flow and knows a victim’s login name can:

* **Capture a victim’s single-use password-reset code** by poisoning the host of the genuine reset email, then **set a new password and take over the account**.
* **Capture invite and email-verification codes** through the same primitive, taking over accounts during onboarding or email-change flows.
* **Take over an instance administrator** (for example `IAM_OWNER`), resulting in full control of the instance.
* **Retain access across a later password rotation**, because once signed in as the victim the attacker can enrol their own credential or second factor.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI, which forwards the public host to the API and builds these links from it, as well as the hosted **Login V1** UI and the API, where links sent by ZITADEL are built from the public host of the request that triggered them. The `x-zitadel-public-host` header is not normalized by a standard fronting proxy, so it can be set by a client even in a typical deployment. The email itself is genuine - correct sender, correct branding, a real code - so only the link host differs; the poisoned link must be fetched once, by the victim opening the link or by automated inbound-mail link scanning.

The attacker does not need the victim’s password, mailbox access, an existing session or any secret, nor any API credentials or instance misconfiguration. The attacker only needs to know one host the instance trusts, such as its own domain. Existing passwords, passkeys, or second factors do not prevent the reset, since completing it sets a new password and yields a live session.

**Scope note:** Exposure is instance-wide - any user on the instance can be targeted, across organizations, but not across instances. This is a bypass of [GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-mchc-246r-6m76), whose fix (`4.19.5`) rejected public hosts that are not trusted, but accepted a trusted host followed by user information and a different host.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.19.5` through `4.20.2` (including RC versions)

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

The patched version only accepts a public host that is a plain host with an optional port - no user information, path, query, or fragment - and rejects a request with an invalid or ambiguous public-host header with `400 Bad Request`, before the trusted-domain check. advisories.title: Account takeover in Login V2 through a forgeable email verification proof
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI let an unauthenticated attacker set the first credential of a user who had none yet, and then sign in as that user. This applies to active users who had not yet set a password, passkey or identity provider link, for example invited users or users created through the API before their first sign-in.

Login V2 remembered that a user had just verified their email address or invite code with a `verificationCheck` cookie. Its value was a SHA-256 hash of the user ID and the browser’s fingerprint cookie, so it consisted only of values that the client controls or can learn. No server-side secret was involved. Anyone could compute a valid value for any user. Login V2 accepted this cookie as proof of a recent verification wherever a user without an authentication method sets up a first credential. The same forgeable proof was therefore reachable through password setup, passkey registration, and linking an external identity provider.

### Impact

An attacker who knows the user ID or login name of a user without any authentication method can:

* **Set the user’s password** without a verification code, and sign in as that user. Login V2 set the password with its own service credential.
* **Register a passkey** for that user, using a session that only identifies the user by login name, and sign in with it.
* **Link the attacker’s own account at an external identity provider** to that user and sign in through it, if an identity provider that allows account linking is configured.

Each vector results in a takeover of the affected account, including its permissions in ZITADEL and its access to every application that uses ZITADEL for sign-in.

Users who already have an authentication method, such as a password, a passkey or an identity provider link, are not affected: Login V2 only accepted the forgeable proof for users without one. Deployments that do not serve the Login V2 UI are not affected.

**Scope note:** The vulnerability is limited to the Login V2 UI and to users of the instance it serves. The ZITADEL APIs themselves were not affected.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.19.4` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. Login V2 now only accepts a verification proof that it issued itself after the backend accepted the email or invite code. The proof is signed with a server-side secret, bound to the user and the browser, and expires after 5 minutes. Values in the old format are rejected. The proof Login V2 uses when linking an identity provider to a signed-in session is signed the same way.

The proofs are signed with `ZITADEL_SESSION_COOKIE_SECRET`. If it is not set, Login V2 derives the key from its configured API credential. Make sure the secret is set to a randomly generated value (at least 32 characters, for example `openssl rand -base64 32`), not a value copied from an example configuration.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.19.5](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.19.5)

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions. As a partial mitigation, create users with an initial credential, so that no active user is left without an authentication method.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

advisories.title: Account Takeover via Header Injection
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI allowed an unauthenticated attacker who knows only a victim’s login name to redirect that victim’s genuine password-reset, invite, and email-verification links to an attacker-controlled host, while the links still carried the real single-use codes. Harvesting such a code lets the attacker set a new password - or complete verification - and sign in as the victim, including an instance administrator.

The login UI built these email links from client-supplied proxy request headers (`x-zitadel-public-host`, `x-zitadel-forward-host`, and `x-forwarded-host`) without confirming the host belonged to the instance, and the API’s trusted-domain control - which is meant to reject an untrusted public host - was silently skipped when the submitted host was malformed in a way that resolved to an empty host (for example a value with a non-numeric port such as `evil.com:443/`). Any of these headers can be used; the issue is not specific to one of them. The shared missing invariant is that a public host taken from a request header is never validated against the instance’s trusted domains before it is used to build a security-sensitive link.

### Impact

An attacker who can reach the unauthenticated Login V2 reset or verification flow and knows a victim’s login name can:

* **Capture a victim’s single-use password-reset code** by poisoning the host of the genuine reset email, then **set a new password and take over the account**.
* **Capture invite and email-verification codes** through the same primitive, taking over accounts during onboarding or email-change flows.
* **Take over an instance administrator** (for example `IAM_OWNER`), resulting in full control of the instance.
* **Retain access across a later password rotation**, because once signed in as the victim the attacker can enrol their own credential or second factor.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML); the `x-zitadel-public-host` and `x-zitadel-forward-host` headers in particular are not normalized by a standard fronting proxy, so the host can be set by a client even in a typical deployment. The email itself is genuine - correct sender, correct branding, a real code - so only the link host differs; the poisoned link must be fetched once, by the victim opening the link or by automated inbound-mail link scanning.

The attacker does not need the victim’s password, mailbox access, an existing session or any secret, nor any API credentials, localhost access, or instance misconfiguration - the default forced-Login V2 deployment is affected. Existing passwords, passkeys, or second factors do not prevent the reset, since completing it sets a new password and yields a live session. Deployments that do **not** run Login V2 (for example Login V1 only) are not affected, as Login V1 does not build these links from the public-host headers.

advisories.title: One-Click Account Takeover through Device Code
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI approved an OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization request as soon as a browser opened its signed-in page for that request, using whichever session the browser already had. The user was neither asked for consent nor required to enter the user code shown on the device. An attacker who starts a device authorization for an application and gets a signed-in user to open a single link receives tokens for that user’s account on the attacker’s device.

Approving a device authorization was not properly authorized. ZITADEL confirmed neither that the user intended to approve this device nor that the user may access the application. The same missing authorization was reachable through the OIDC service API that login UIs use to approve device authorizations (`POST /v2/oidc/device_authorization/{device_authorization_id}`). That endpoint skipped the project access settings that the regular sign-in enforces.

### Impact

An attacker who can start a device authorization for an application with the Device Code grant type can:

* **Take over a user’s session for that application with one click.** The attacker sends the user a link to the Login V2 signed-in page carrying the attacker’s user code. If the user is signed in to Login V2 in that browser, opening the link approves the attacker’s device, with no further interaction. The attacker’s device then receives the access, ID and (if requested) refresh tokens of that user, with the scopes the attacker requested.
* **Gain API access as that user.** If the attacker requests the ZITADEL project scope, the tokens can be used against the ZITADEL APIs with all permissions of that user. For an administrator, this means administrative control over the organization or instance.
* **Bypass the project access settings.** Approving a device authorization through the API did not check the project settings “Only authorized users can authenticate” and “Authentication is restricted to users from organizations that have been granted access to this project”. Users without the required roles, or from organizations without a project grant, could obtain tokens for the application through the Device Authorization flow.

The attacker cannot read the user’s password or second factors, and cannot approve a device without the user opening the link in a browser with an active Login V2 session.

Instances without any application that has the Device Code grant type are not affected, as no device authorization can be started. Users who sign in only through the hosted **Login V1** UI are not affected by the one-click vector, as they have no Login V2 session that the link could reuse.

**Scope note:** The first vector affects deployments that run the hosted Login V2 UI. The API vector also affects custom login UIs built on the OIDC service API. Both vectors stay within a single instance.

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. Approving a device authorization through the API now enforces the same project access settings as the regular sign-in.

advisories.title: Unauthenticated Account Takeover Through Predictable Session IDs
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI allowed an unauthenticated attacker to obtain a fresh session token for another user’s authenticated session - including every factor that user had completed, such as MFA - without a password, a second factor, an existing session token, or any interaction with the victim, provided the attacker could guess the victim’s session ID. Session IDs are time-ordered identifiers, so an attacker who creates sessions shortly before and after the victim signs in can narrow the candidates to a small set and test them.

Login V2 kept its session references in a browser cookie that was neither signed nor otherwise validated. When updating a session, the login UI forwarded the session ID from that cookie to the session API using its own service-user credentials, which hold the `session.write` permission; the session API accepts such updates without the session’s current token and returns a newly issued one. As a result, a forged cookie entry containing a guessed session ID and an empty token was sufficient to make the login UI rotate - and hand out - the token of a session it had not created.

### Impact

An attacker who can reach the Login V2 UI and can estimate when a victim signs in can:

* **Obtain a valid session token for the victim’s authenticated session**, retaining every factor the victim completed, including MFA.
* **Act as the victim** - complete OIDC and SAML flows and call ZITADEL’s APIs with that token. If the victim is an instance administrator (e.g. `IAM_OWNER`), this results in full instance takeover; for a non-privileged victim it is a takeover of that user’s account.
* **Read the details of any session by its ID** (login name, authentication factors) and **sign that session out**, through the same unsigned cookie.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML).

The attack is timing-sensitive: the attacker must guess the session ID from a window around the victim’s sign-in. The time-based structure of session IDs narrows that search, while load balancing, concurrent traffic and any rate limiting in front of the login UI widen it. It does **not** require the victim to do anything beyond signing in normally, and it does **not** depend on how the victim authenticates - password, passkey and external identity provider logins all produce the same kind of session. Deployments that do **not** run Login V2 (for example Login V1 only) are not affected: the session API itself only accepts token-less updates from callers holding `session.write` (`IAM_OWNER` and `IAM_LOGIN_CLIENT`), which are not exposed to end users.

**Scope note:** This affects the **Login V2** UI only; the session API’s behaviour is unchanged and by design. Exposure is instance-wide - any session on the instance can be targeted, across organizations, but not across instances. It is the login-side counterpart of [GHSA-6c5p-6www-pcmr](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-6c5p-6www-pcmr), which restricted token-less session updates to callers with `session.write`: that permission is legitimately held by the login UI, and this issue is the login UI applying it to a session ID chosen by the client. Operators of a custom login built on the session API with a `session.write` service user should verify that it only acts on session IDs it issued itself. It is independent of [GHSA-3gwm-5wx8-4gm6](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/security/advisories/GHSA-3gwm-5wx8-4gm6), which concerns OTP challenge handling.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.19.1` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases.

advisories.title: SAML Identity-Provider Confusion in ZITADEL Leads to Account Takeover
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s SAML identity-provider **intent** callback (the endpoint used by **Login V2** and custom login UIs to complete an external SAML login) accepted an assertion signed by one configured SAML identity provider as proof of identity for a login started against a *different* SAML identity provider.

On an instance with two or more SAML identity providers, an attacker who can configure one SAML identity provider and controls its signing key could complete a login intent aimed at a second SAML identity provider and obtain an authenticated session as any user linked to that second provider, without any interaction from the victim. The callback selected the identity provider whose certificate verifies the assertion’s signature from the request URL, but resolved the local user account from the login intent, and never checked that the two identity providers were the same.

### Impact

An attacker who can configure a SAML identity provider on the instance and controls that provider’s signing key can:

- **Obtain an authenticated session as any user** linked to a *different* SAML identity provider on the same instance
- **Impersonate that user** in every application that relies on the instance for authentication
- Do so **without victim interaction**, and without ever completing a login at the victim’s identity provider

This affects instances that have **two or more SAML identity providers** configured, where at least one user is linked to one of them (normal once a user has signed in through that provider). The flaw is reachable through the identity-provider **intent** flow used by **Login V2** and by custom login UIs built on the session API.

Configuring an identity provider requires organization-administrator permission (`org.idp.write`). Registering the attacker’s provider is cheap: only identity-provider metadata containing a certificate whose private key the attacker holds is needed, and no running identity provider is required. On self-hosted deployments that ship with public organization registration enabled, an otherwise unauthenticated attacker can gain organization-administrator permission by registering an organization. On ZITADEL Cloud, public organization registration is disabled, so the attacker must already be an organization administrator on the instance.

Accounts that authenticate only through non-SAML providers (OIDC, Google, GitHub, JWT) or through local credentials are **not** affected, because the confused flow requires a SAML-targeted login intent, so only users linked to a SAML identity provider are reachable. Instances with fewer than two SAML identity providers have nothing to confuse. The issue does **not** by itself grant administrative permissions; its impact is impersonation of, and session takeover for, the targeted user.

**Scope note:** This affects the SAML identity-provider intent flow only. It is instance-wide and crosses organizations (an administrator of any one organization can target users in any other organization on the same instance), but it does **not** cross instances (all lookups are instance-scoped). **Login V1**’s external-login callback is not affected, because it selects the identity provider from the server-side login request rather than from the callback URL.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.19.1` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. The SAML assertion callback now verifies that the identity provider named in the callback URL is the same identity provider the login intent was started for, and rejects the callback when they differ. The same check is applied to the SAML single-logout callback.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.19.2](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.19.2)

advisories.title: IAM_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR allows to impersonate all users, including IAM_OWNER
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s OIDC token exchange allowed a user holding only the end-user impersonation permission to impersonate administrators, including an instance owner (`IAM_OWNER`).

ZITADEL distinguishes two impersonation permissions: `impersonation`, granted by the `IAM_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` and `ORG_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` roles, is documented to allow impersonating end users only, while impersonating administrators additionally requires `admin.impersonation`, granted by the `IAM_ADMIN_IMPERSONATOR` and `ORG_ADMIN_IMPERSONATOR` roles. The token exchange only ever checked `impersonation` and never whether the impersonated user is an administrator, so `admin.impersonation` was not enforced.

### Impact

An actor holding one of the `*_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` roles can:

- **Impersonate any administrator** within the scope of their role (instance-wide for `IAM_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR`, the users of their organization for `ORG_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR`), including `IAM_OWNER` and `ORG_OWNER`
- **Sign in to applications as that administrator**, with the administrator’s roles and claims

Impersonated tokens are marked as such and are rejected by ZITADEL’s own APIs, so the issue does **not** grant access to the ZITADEL Console or the management APIs. Its impact is limited to what the impersonated administrator can do in applications that rely on the instance for authentication.

This affects instances where impersonation is enabled (the instance security setting *Allow Impersonation*, which is disabled by default, and the token exchange grant on at least one application) and where at least one user holds an `*_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` role. Exploitation requires that role, so it is only reachable by users an administrator has already trusted to impersonate end users.

**Scope note:** A user counts as an administrator as soon as they hold any membership (instance, organization, project or project grant). The issue does not cross organizations for `ORG_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` and does not cross instances.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.19.1` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. Impersonating a user who holds any membership now requires the `admin.impersonation` permission, which only the `IAM_ADMIN_IMPERSONATOR` and `ORG_ADMIN_IMPERSONATOR` roles grant; the `*_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` roles can only impersonate users without memberships.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.19.2](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.19.2)

The **3.x** release line reached end-of-life on 2026-08-31 and will not receive a fix for this vulnerability. Affected 3.x deployments must upgrade to a patched 4.x release.

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. On unpatched versions, the issue can be avoided by not granting the `IAM_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` and `ORG_END_USER_IMPERSONATOR` roles, or by disabling impersonation in the instance security settings.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to Wojciech Piekutowski from Nedap for finding and reporting the vulnerability.

advisories.title: Unauthenticated attacker can rename any user (including admins) through the login V1
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V1** UI allowed an unauthenticated attacker who knows only a victim’s login name to permanently change that account’s username. By starting an ordinary login flow, submitting the victim’s login name to identify the account, and then posting a new username, the attacker could rename any active human user on the instance - including administrators - without ever supplying a password or any second factor.

The change-username request acted on the account bound to the login flow as soon as a login name had been entered, before the flow had reached the change-username step and before any authentication factor had been verified.

### Impact

An attacker with only network access to the hosted **Login V1** UI and knowledge of a victim’s login name can:

- **Rename any active human account** on the instance, across every organization, including instance administrators
- **Lock the victim out** of their account, because the identifier they previously logged in with no longer resolves to them
- **Free the victim’s former login name for re-registration**, where the organization’s login policy permits self-registration or domain discovery, enabling squatting of the released identifier

This affects deployments that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V1** UI (OIDC/SAML).

On its own this issue does **not** grant account takeover: no password, session, or token is disclosed, and the attacker cannot authenticate as the victim. The impact is to **integrity** (unauthorized modification of account identifiers) and **availability** (lockout of the legitimate owner). **Machine and service accounts are not affected**, because the login-name step binds only active human users, so a non-human account cannot be selected as the rename target through this flow. The standalone **Login V2** application does not expose this change-username flow and is not vulnerable through it.

**Scope note:** This is an instance-wide, cross-organization flaw on the hosted **Login V1** surface: any active human in any organization on the instance can be renamed by an anonymous caller. It does not cross instance boundaries. It shares its root cause with `GHSA-72q5-mv5c-vxv4` - a **Login V1** flow handler that acted on the account bound by login name before the flow had reached the relevant step or verified a factor, fixed the same way by gating the handler on the flow’s current step. That advisory covered unauthenticated MFA enrollment and phone-number overwrite; this one covers the username change.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.17.3` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. The hosted **Login V1** UI now performs a username change only once the login flow has legitimately reached the change-username step, which is presented only after the first factor and any required multi-factor checks have succeeded. A request that has merely identified an account by login name can no longer trigger a rename.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [`v4.19.1`](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.19.1)

⚠️ Please skip the v4.18.0 release and use v4.19.1. The setup step fails in this version (https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/issues/12780).

The **3.x** release line reached end-of-life on 2026-08-31 and will not receive a fix for this vulnerability. Affected 3.x deployments must upgrade to a patched 4.x release.

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at security@zitadel.com

### Credits

Thanks to Adam Korczynski (Ada Logics) for reporting the vulnerability.

advisories.title: Cross-user session hijacking and external IdP token theft via forgeable IdP intent tokens
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL issues an **IdP intent** token to the login UI after a user completes a login with an external identity provider (IdP). The login UI presents this token, together with the intent’s identifier, to retrieve the result of the external login and to authenticate the user’s session. These tokens were protected with an unauthenticated, malleable encryption mode, so their integrity was not cryptographically verified when they were redeemed.

An authenticated attacker with a valid account on the same instance who also knew a target intent’s identifier could take a token they legitimately obtained for their own intent and modify it into a token that the backend accepted for a *different* intent. Because the token was validated only by decrypting it and comparing the result to the supplied intent identifier - with no authentication tag or signature - a tampered token whose decrypted value matched was treated as genuine.

### Impact

An attacker who holds a valid account on the instance, and who can predict a victim’s in-flight external-login intent identifier and win a short timing race against that login, can:

- **Read another user’s external-login result**, including the **IdP access, ID, and refresh tokens** returned for that login, by calling the intent-information endpoint (`POST /v2/idp_intents/{id}`) with a forged intent token. Depending on the external provider and requested scopes, those tokens may grant further access to the victim’s third-party resources.
- **Hijack the victim’s pending session**, by consuming the succeeded intent before the victim does (via `POST /v2/sessions`) and obtaining a session that ZITADEL treats as authenticated **as the victim**.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s external IdP login using a custom login UI or the session API (including **Login V2**).

The attack is probabilistic and time-bounded, which materially narrows real-world exposure. The intent identifier is a Sonyflake value that the attacker must predict to within roughly a 10-millisecond window; the attacker must then win a race against the victim’s own redemption inside the login window and brute-force the trailing ciphertext bytes. The reporter estimated on the order of a 1.25% success probability within a 15-second window, and ZITADEL Cloud’s per-IP rate limiting and bot detection reduce feasibility further. Instances that do **not** use external identity providers are **not** affected, because no IdP intent tokens are ever issued; the flaw only concerns the external-login intent flow and does not by itself expose stored credentials or data for users who are not actively performing an external IdP login.

**Scope note:** The flaw affects the external **IdP intent** flow only. It is an instance-wide issue - any authenticated user on an instance could target another user’s in-flight external login on that same instance - and does not cross instance boundaries.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.17.2` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. IdP intent tokens are now protected with authenticated encryption (`A256GCM`): any modification to a token is detected and the token is rejected, so a valid token can no longer be forged by tampering with a token obtained for a different intent.

advisories.title: Unauthenticated Account Takeover Through External Identity Provider with Account Manual Linking enabled
advisories.summary:
### Summary

ZITADEL established links between user accounts and external identity providers without verifying that the requester was entitled to create the link. The hosted **Login V2** UI accepted explicit IdP linking on an identify-only session - created by merely submitting a login name, with no factor verified - allowing an unauthenticated attacker who knows only a victim’s login name to bind their own external identity to the victim’s account and then sign in through that identity provider as the victim. The same missing verification was reachable directly through the User Service V2 **`AddIDPLink`** endpoint (`POST /v2/users/{user_id}/links`), which skipped the permission check whenever a caller targeted their own account, letting any authenticated user bind an unverified external identity. On both paths, the link was created before any check that a primary factor had been verified or that the caller held the required permission.

### Impact

An attacker who knows a victim’s login name, in an organization that permits external IdP account linking, can:

- **Bind their own external identity to the victim’s account**, by driving Login V2’s explicit-linking flow against an identify-only session (login name submitted, no factor verified)
- **Sign in as the victim** through that identity provider afterward, obtaining a fully authenticated session

Through the API surface of the same flaw, any authenticated user - without knowing anyone’s login name - can **pre-claim an arbitrary external identity on their own account** via `AddIDPLink`. Because external IdP links are globally unique (first claim wins), this diverts or blocks the victim’s future federated logins, though this vector alone does not authenticate the attacker as the victim.

This affects applications that authenticate users through ZITADEL’s hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML); the API vector additionally affects any deployment exposing the User Service V2 API, independent of which login UI is used.

The attack does not require the attacker to know or guess the victim’s password, existing authenticators, or MFA - the identify-only session alone is sufficient. **Login V1 is not affected**: it executes linking only after the target account has completed primary-factor and MFA verification.

**Scope note:** The flaw is instance-wide/cross-organization but not cross-instance. Both attack vectors stem from the same missing verification when establishing an external-identity link and are fixed together in one release.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.17.2` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.15` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. Patched versions enforce the same rule on every path that establishes an external-identity link: Login V2 authorizes explicit IdP linking through the same guard used for authenticator enrollment (a verified, non-expired primary factor on the session, or - for a user with no authentication methods yet - a passed user-verification check bound to the browser’s fingerprint), and `AddIDPLink` enforces its permission check unconditionally, including when the caller targets their own account.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.17.3](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.17.3)

The **3.x** release line reached end-of-life on 2026-08-31 and will not receive a fix for this vulnerability. Affected 3.x deployments must upgrade to a patched 4.x release.

### Workarounds

The recommended solution is to upgrade to a patched version. There is no configuration that fully closes this gap on unpatched versions. As a partial mitigation, disabling external IdP account linking in an affected organization’s login policy closes the Login V2 vector; it does not close the API vector, which is independent of login-policy configuration.
